title: Asking politely
topic: אֶפְשָׁר…?; בְּבַקָּשָׁה; the everyday imperative (תַּגִּיד, תַּגִּידִי)
why: With no formal "you," Hebrew is polite in other ways: אֶפְשָׁר, תּוּכַל / תּוּכְלִי and a few soft imperatives learned as set phrases. This lesson prepares the role-play in the review.

{"lessons": ["

No formal \"you\": how do you stay polite?

Like English, Hebrew has no formal \"you\": you speak the same way to everyone, the driver, the shop assistant, your boss. Politeness comes from the way you ask. The magic word: אֶפְשָׁר…? (efshar, \"is it possible?\").

אֶפְשָׁר מַיִם, בְּבַקָּשָׁה?Could I have some water, please? [efshar mayim, bevakasha?]

Followed by an infinitive, אֶפְשָׁר is used to ask permission, with no pronoun and no agreement:

אֶפְשָׁר לָשֶׁבֶת פֹּה?Can I sit here? [efshar lashevet po?]
סְלִיחָה, אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲבֹר?Excuse me, can I get by? [slikha, efshar la'avor?]
אֶפְשָׁר לָרֶדֶת בַּתַּחֲנָה הַבָּאָה?Can I get off at the next stop? [efshar laredet ba-takhana ha-ba'a?]

בְּבַקָּשָׁה means \"please,\" but also \"you're welcome\" when someone thanks you, and \"here you go\" when you hand something over.

", "

Could you…? Tell me…

As in English (\"could you help me?\"), you soften a request with תּוּכַל (to a man) / תּוּכְלִי (to a woman) + infinitive:

תּוּכַל לַעֲזֹר לִי?Could you help me? (to a man) [tukhal la'azor li?]
תּוּכְלִי לְדַבֵּר לְאַט?Could you speak slowly? (to a woman) [tukhli ledaber le'at?]

To say \"come\" or \"wait,\" Israelis very often use a future form instead of the imperative, which sounds softer. For now, learn them as set phrases; for a woman, you add ִי.

To a manTo a womanMeaning
תַּגִּיד tagidתַּגִּידִי tagiditell (me)
תָּבוֹא tavoתָּבוֹאִי tavo'icome
תְּחַכֶּה רֶגַע tekhake regaתְּחַכִּי רֶגַע tekhaki regawait a moment

תַּגִּיד… at the start of a sentence is the \"tell me…\" that opens a question: תַּגִּיד, אֵיפֹה הַתַּחֲנָה?

", "

Thanks, sorry, no problem

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
תּוֹדָה רַבָּהtoda rabathank you very much
בְּבַקָּשָׁהbevakashaplease; you're welcome
אֵין בְּעָיָהein be'ayano problem
סְלִיחָהslikhasorry, excuse me
אֲנִי לֹא מֵבִין / מְבִינָהani lo mevin / mevinaI don't understand (m. / f.)
עוֹד פַּעַם?od pa'am?one more time?
סְלִיחָה, אֲנִי לֹא מְבִינָה. עוֹד פַּעַם, לְאַט?Sorry, I don't understand. One more time, slowly? [slikha, ani lo mevina. od pa'am, le'at?]

Israelis speak fast and directly: it isn't rudeness. Don't hesitate to ask for לְאַט (slowly): you'll often hear אֵין בְּעָיָה in reply.
